newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Rain threatens E Europe cereals crop. [CORRECTED 15:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rain threatens E Europe cereals crop. [CORRECTED 15:30 GMT]

text.p: Central and Eastern Europe have been expected in the grain trade to deliver far bigger harvests this year than in 1996, but rain across the region has introduced an element of doubt.

Heavy rain has hit Poland and the Czech Republic, triggered grain price rises in Hungary and slowed the Serbian harvest. Bulgarian officials are cutting harvest ideas, after bad weather in June. Slovakia's rapeseed harvest has been halted by bad weather.

According to estimates from the London-based International Grains Council, the region will produce 33.9 million tonnes of wheat this year, compared to 1996's disappointing 26.2 million. But this still leaves the crop well under 1995's 35.4 million tonnes.
"Last year was very bad. It doesn't take much to increase it," one London-based economist said.
According to the IGC's estimates earlier this month, Romania may see the biggest increase, with a crop more than doubling from 3.2 million tonnes in 1996 to 7.8 million this year.
Romania hopes to bring in 7.07 million tonnes of wheat this year, despite rain damage, according to Adorian Kovacs, State Secretary at the Agriculture Ministry.

Hungary, eyed by some western European traders as a potential exporter in the new season, will increase its wheat crop by 1.1 million tonnes, to 5.0 million tonnes (corrects from 3.9 million tonnes), asccording to IGC estimates.
Even before the latest flooding, the IGC predicted a fall in the Polish wheat crop, from 8.5 million tonnes in 1996, to 8.2 million this year.
Analysts in Poland reckoned grain output may be reduced slightly by recent flooding in wheat-rich south-western regions, but losses will be contained if the rains stop soon.
They had forecast this year's total grain crop to be roughly equal to or just below the 24.7 million tonnes produced in 1996, with estimates ranging from about 23.5-25 million tonnes.

"It seems forecasts of the grain harvest falling some two to three percent are realistic, with much larger falls...not probable despite all this rain," said Andrzej Kalicki, analyst at Warsaw Commodities Exchange.
But analysts said output might be reduced significantly if rains persisted and flooding continued,

"Flooding will cause losses in the south-west, but it is too early to put an exact figure on it," said one, adding that losses should amount to less than five percent if weather patterns returned to normal.
A spokesman for the agriculture ministry said no official crop loss estimates would be given until water levels dropped and fields were examined, which could take days.

Over the past fews days heavy downpours have resulted in flooding in many parts of southern Poland, and flooding in the eastern Czech Republic this week will result in large agricultural losses, officials said. They said it was too early to estimate the full extent of damage.
Milos Kordac, an assistant to the president of the Czech Agrarian Chamber, said that "there will be large losses... but it is too early for even early estimates".
He said Northern Moravia, the region worst hit by the flooding, was a grain, potato and sugar beet growing area.
Libuse Alterova of the Agricultural Ministry press department said more damage could follow as the flood wave was moving downstream on the Morava river to fertile area in southern Moravia.
In Hungary, milling wheat futures rose on the Budapest Commodity Exchange on Tuesday on fears of low-quality crops, traders said.
"Dealers...were afraid the rains could endanger the quality of the wheat crop," said Antal Szoke of Agrimpex.
Showers and cold weather hit Hungary last weekend but forecasters said conditions were likely to change by the second half of the week.
Rain and hail in some parts of Serbia over the past few days have slowed wheat harvesting and could reduce yields in those areas by several percent, Belgrade media reported on Tuesday.
"When weather is as rainy as it is now, wheat yields are several percent lower every day," Srbislav Dencic of the Novi Sad Institute for Crop Farming was quoted as saying by the daily Nasa Borba.
According to Dencic, it was impossible to say how much would be lost since detailed information was needed on the levels of rain and hail.
"In any case, such weather postpones harvesting and yield could generally be 10 to 15 percent lower," Dencic said.

The highest rainfall since Saturday, with hail in places, was registered in the granary of Vojvodina, where wheat harvesting began a few days ago on some 366,000 hectares of the total 800,000 ha under wheat in Yugoslavia.
Vojvodina is expected to account for some 1.358 million of Yugoslavia's total wheat crop of 2.75 million tonnes.
However, the rains may benefit spring crops such as maize.
Cooler, cloudy and windy weather with occasional showers will continue until Thursday, when a sunny and dry spell with a slight rise in temperatures is expected, forecasters said.
Bulgaria's agriculture ministry said on Tuesday the wheat harvest was on schedule but may be lower than expected due to bad weather.
"The ministry forecast wheat output of 2.4 million tonnes in May, but due to hailstorms and heavy rains last month the harvest may be lower," a ministry spokeswoman said.
She said it was too early to make new forecasts from the yields of wheat harvested so far as the harvest began only 10 days ago.
The ministry said 33,557 hectares of wheat and 168,289 ha of barley had been harvested so far, which amounted to 2.74 and 59 percent of sown areas.
Some 32,000 ha planted to wheat and barley and 16,000 ha planted to spring crops such as maize, sunflower and sugar beet were damaged by the storms, ministry data showed.
